newsitem.title: BELGIUM: World polio victory delayed, measles on way out.
newsitem.headline: World polio victory delayed, measles on way out.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
The race to rid the world of polio has slowed, but measles may soon join smallpox as an eradicated killer disease, a conference was told Thursday.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) said back in 1988 that poliomyelitis, a deformer and killer of children, would be defeated by 2000, but this has slipped back five years.
"The eradication of polio is clearly within our grasp. We only need to sustain the will for the world to be certified free of polio by 2005," Dr Harry Hull from WHO told a conference.
Hull told the conference, Global Immunisation, organised by Anglo-American drugs giant SmithKline Beecham Plc, that other scourges of the world's children are close to being beaten back for good.
Asked at a press conference, which diseases would join smallpox in the viral museum, Hull pointed to Guinea Worm, mainly affecting African communities, and measles.
"Guinea worm is about to be eliminated, and also in theory, there's a growing movement, I wouldn't call it a consensus yet, that measles could be next," Hull said.

Measles remains one of the major childhood killers - accounting for more child deaths than any other vaccine- preventible illness. WHO estimates that more than a million children died from measles in 1994. 98 per cent of these deaths occur in developing countries.
The effort to eradicate polio is currently being stepped up.
In three weeks India will attempt to vaccinate 125 million children aged under five in one day, Hull said. Last January Indian authorities vaccinated 93 million children in a day.
Last year almost half the world's children under five, a record 300 million, were immunised against polio, an acute, infectious viral disease transmitted mainly because of inadequate sewage.
Polio infection can lead to fever, paralysis or death. Victims of the disease, just about eradicated in north America and western Europe, now mainly come from the third world.
Last year 7,000 cases were reported worldwide, but according to Dr Hull the actual occurrence was about 70,000, and without immunisation there would be about 600,000 cases a year.
Hull said to keep the polio-free world programme on target, governments will have to spend between $600 and $800 million by 2005.

"Since 1978 the world has saved about $20 billion as polio has been steadily defeated. The savings would equal $1.5 billion a year in the case of eradication, from not having to provide vaccination," Hull said.
In another speech to the conference, Dr Walter Orenstein, form the Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta, Georgia, said immunisation has had a major impact on disease prevention.
"WHO estimates that over 157 million cases of measles, pertussis (whooping cough) and polio and over 2.9 million deaths were prevented in 1994 alone," Orenstein said.
Opening the conference, Jean Stephenne, general manager of SmithKline Beecham Biologicals, said the future for new vaccines was promising.
"There is currently a revolution going on in the development of new vaccines," Stephenne said.

New products will address modern problems induced by increasing foreign travel and people living longer. Teenagers will receive protection from the potentialy fatal liver disease Hepatitis B, and against sexually transmitted diseases like Herpes. The elderly will be protected against traditional winter killers like influenza, according to Stephenne.
"In the next decade vaccination will also be increasingly possible against cancer and malaria," Stephenne said.
